youtube.aciklama:
We explain what sound is from the ground up: vibration, compression and rarefaction, longitudinal waves, the speed of sound in different media, and why sound cannot travel in a vacuum. We also take a short look at how sound passes from air to solid to fluid inside the ear.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Speaks, Introduction to Sound: Acoustics for the Hearing and Speech Sciences; Gelfand, Hearing: An Introduction to Psychological and Physiological Acoustics; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
With this lesson we start sound physics: we will learn what sound is, how it is produced and how it travels.
We will look at vibration, compression and rarefaction, longitudinal waves, and why sound cannot travel in a vacuum.
Sound is a form of energy that travels through the vibration of molecules in a medium.
First, sound needs a vibrating source, such as a tuning fork, a loudspeaker cone or the vocal folds.
The second condition is a medium to carry the vibration, such as air, water or bone.
For hearing, a third thing is needed: a receiver to detect the vibration, such as an ear or a microphone.
In physics, sound exists even if no one hears it; hearing is the perception of sound by a living being.
Vibration is the back and forth movement of an object around its rest position.
When we strike a tuning fork, its prongs begin to swing quickly outward and inward.
As the prongs move outward, they push the nearby air molecules and crowd them together.
As the prongs move back inward, they leave behind a region where the molecules are more spread out.
The motion continues thanks to two properties: elasticity pulls the object back, and its mass makes it overshoot the rest position.
This regular, single-frequency motion is called simple harmonic motion; this is how a tuning fork produces a pure tone.
Friction uses up some energy in each cycle, so the vibration fades over time; this is called damping.
As the tuning fork keeps vibrating, regions of compression and rarefaction follow one another away from the source.
The region where molecules crowd together and pressure rises slightly is called compression, or condensation.
The region where molecules spread apart and pressure drops slightly is called rarefaction.
At the top of the screen you see how the molecules are spread out, and below, the pressure change measured at the same moment.
The peaks of the pressure curve correspond to compressions, and the troughs to rarefactions.
This curve is the most common way to show sound, but sound itself is not a wavy line; it is a pressure change in the air.
Here is an important point: as sound travels, air molecules do not travel all the way from the source to the ear.
Each molecule only moves back and forth over a short distance around its own rest position and passes the motion to its neighbor.
What travels is not the molecules themselves but the pattern of compression and rarefaction, that is, energy.
Think of the wave in a stadium: the fans stand up and sit down in place, but the wave moves around the stands.
So sound is not a flow of air like wind; wind is air being carried from one place to another.
A spring toy shows the same thing: the coils swing in place, while the compressed region moves along the spring.

ogeler.metin: Motion along the direction of travel

cumleler: Waves fall into two groups, depending on the direction in which the particles move.
In a longitudinal wave, the particles move back and forth along the same line as the direction of travel.
Sound in air is a longitudinal wave; compression and rarefaction can only form with this kind of motion.
In a transverse wave, the particles move at right angles to the direction of travel; a wave on a stretched rope is an example.
In liquids and gases, sound travels only as a longitudinal wave, while in solids transverse waves can also form.
In the traveling wave of the cochlea, the basilar membrane moves up and down; we will see this in later lessons.
To describe a sound wave, we look at a few basic properties.
Frequency is the number of vibrations per second, and it is related to whether we hear a sound as low or high in pitch.
Amplitude is the size of the pressure change, and it is related to perceived loudness.
Wavelength is the distance from one compression to the next.
We will study these properties in detail in the next two lessons.
Sound does not travel at the same speed in every medium; its speed depends on the stiffness and density of the medium.
In air at twenty degrees Celsius, sound travels about three hundred forty three meters per second.
Speed rises as air warms; at zero degrees it drops to about three hundred thirty one meters, changing about point six meters per degree.
In water, sound is about four times faster: about one thousand four hundred eighty meters per second.
In hard solids such as steel, the speed rises above five thousand meters per second.
Solids are denser, but they are much stiffer, that is, harder to compress, so sound travels faster in them.
Counting from lightning to thunder is an everyday example of this speed: every three seconds is about one kilometer.

maddeler.metin: _Taken into account_ in tests like ABR

cumleler: Knowing the speed of sound is also useful in the clinic.
With insert earphones, sound travels from the transducer to the ear through a thin tube, adding a delay of about point nine milliseconds.
This delay is taken into account in tests measured in milliseconds, such as the auditory brainstem response, or ABR.
In sound field testing, a distance of one meter between the loudspeaker and the head means a delay of about three milliseconds.
The brain also uses the fact that sound reaches the two ears at different times to locate a sound; we will see this later.
Since sound is carried by the vibration of molecules, it cannot travel where there are no molecules.
In a classic seventeenth-century experiment, as the air is pumped out of a glass jar, the sound of the bell inside slowly fades away.
The bell keeps vibrating, but there is no air left to carry the vibration to the ear.
This is also why sound cannot travel in space; astronauts talk by radio, that is, with electromagnetic waves.
Light and radio waves are electromagnetic waves and can travel in a vacuum, while sound is a mechanical wave.
In short, sound needs a medium: air, water, bone or another material.
The ear itself is a pathway where sound passes through different media.
Sound travels through air in the ear canal and sets the tympanic membrane, the eardrum, into vibration.
In the middle ear, the vibration is carried by solid structures, the ossicular chain.
In the inner ear, the vibration passes into the fluid inside the cochlea.
Most of the energy can be reflected when passing from air to fluid; we will see how the middle ear solves this problem in later lessons.
Sound can also reach the inner ear directly through the skull bones; bone conduction hearing is based on this.
This is also one reason our recorded voice sounds strange to us: when we speak, we hear our voice through both air and bone.

sahneler.metin: Hold the tuning fork only by its stem; touching the prongs damps the vibration. Strike it gently on a rubber pad or your knee, not a hard surface.
cumleler: A useful tip when working with a tuning fork: hold the fork only by its stem.
As soon as you touch the prongs, the vibration is damped and the sound disappears at once.
Strike the fork gently on a rubber pad or on your knee, not on a hard surface; a hard strike can produce unwanted extra tones.
We will look at tuning fork tests in detail in later lessons.
Sound is energy that a vibrating source spreads through the molecules of a medium.
In air, sound is a longitudinal wave made of compressions and rarefactions; the molecules oscillate in place.

sahneler.aciklama: Sound is a _mechanical_ wave; it cannot travel without molecules to carry the vibration.
